question: When a container's very first population fails, the failure is swallowed rather than delivered: every caller already waiting on that first settled state - a callback registered before the failure, a promise someone is awaiting - never learns the attempt failed, and the container is left facing outward as still-loading forever. Worse, once the container is explicitly marked as having failed, nothing it does afterward - not even a fully successful retry - is allowed to bring it back to a working state; the failure is a one-way door. The same two-part contract, delivered exactly once and never a dead end, is honored deliberately elsewhere in the folder: an asynchronous outcome must reach everyone who registered for the first settlement of a value, and a later successful attempt must be able to undo an earlier failure rather than being permanently blocked by it. Which files implement the one-way trap that has to be reopened, and which own the deliver-once / recoverable-afterward machinery it needs to match?

grader_notes.why_cross_repo: ANCHOR (real bug, TanStack/db PR #1751 'fix(db): propagate initial query errors', merged 2026-08-21 as c521b5d6503d - AFTER the pinned commit, verified bug-live-at-pin by direct read of the pin, not just the fix's diff pre-image: at the pin, CollectionLifecycleManager.validTransitions declares `error: ['cleaned-up','idle']` - there is NO error->ready edge - and there is no markError() method at all; onFirstReadyCallbacks (an array of callbacks registered via onFirstReady()) is drained ONLY inside markReady(), so a sync that fails before its first successful commit never calls any registered callback and the collection is stuck in `loading` or an unrecoverable `error` forever. The fix adds markError()/syncError tracking, widens the transition table to error->ready, and threads AbortSignal-aware settlement through collection/sync.ts, collection-config-builder.ts (per-source error tracking distinguishing a fatal top-level error from a recoverable per-source one, plus 'no transition can be missed between observation and subscription' exactly-once registration), subset-dedupe.ts (a deduplicating in-flight-request observer must not treat the ORIGINAL caller's transport failure as its own), and all five collection adapters (electric, powersync, query-db-collection, rxdb, trailbase) which each independently wire their backend's error/ready events into this same lifecycle surface. ECOSYSTEM (reference-correct implementations of the same two-part contract, verified by direct source read at each repo's own pin, not merely mentioned): query.ts's #dispatch reducer has NO guard on the 'fetch' transition - a query can move error->fetching->success unconditionally (recoverable-afterward), and every dispatch runs inside notifyManager.batch so ALL registered observers, not just the first, hear about the transition (deliver-once semantics enforced by React Query's own architecture, not by this file, but this file is where the transition table would have to change if it ever grew a db-style guard). jotai's unwrap.ts explicitly implements the recoverable half with a comment naming the hazard - 'ignore previous errors to avoid getting stuck in error state' - inside the atom read that re-derives PromiseAndValue on every dependency change, and settles promiseErrorCache/promiseResultCache exactly once per promise identity via the `promise !== prev?.p` guard before re-subscribing .then(). redux-toolkit's createAsyncThunk.ts dispatches independent pending/fulfilled/rejected action creators with no state-machine gate at all - Redux reducers are pure functions of the current state and a rejected thunk can always be re-dispatched, so recoverability is structural rather than something this file could get wrong, but it is the reference createAsyncThunk implementations elsewhere in the ecosystem (RTK Query's own build-on-top) inherit from. tldraw's TLSyncClient.ts guards its first-load callback with a `didLoad` boolean exactly analogous to db's onFirstReadyCallbacks-drained-once-in-markReady, and its onStatusChange handler calls config.onSyncError exactly once per transition into the 'error' socket status before closing, rather than leaving callers to poll.
